name: Staff Wellbeing, Time, and Retention
title: Staff Wellbeing, Time, and Retention
answer: AI is often promoted as a way to cut teacher workload, but the evidence that it actually frees up time is mixed, because saved time tends to be absorbed by other demands unless leaders deliberately decide where it goes. The book's answer is a time savings audit tied to reinvestment, made with teachers and written down, alongside staff surveys that lead to visible action and retention analysis used only to offer support. This matters because burnout and turnover are serious problems and workload is a major cause, so any workload claim needs to be checked and any staff data needs clear limits.

sections.body: This idea concerns staff wellbeing, time and retention, and it starts from the fact that teacher burnout and turnover are serious problems with workload as a major cause. AI has been promoted as a way to reduce that workload, but the book treats the claim with caution rather than assuming it holds. The problem it solves is that time savings can look real on paper while changing nothing in practice, because the freed time is quietly taken up by other demands. The book's response is to tie any time savings to a deliberate reinvestment decision, made with teachers and written down, so that savings become real rather than disappearing. It pairs this with staff surveys that feed into action and retention analysis that is used only to support people.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, the starting point is a simple time study of the kind described in Chapter 17, which shows where time is actually going. Leaders then add a decision about where any saved time should go, and that decision is made together with teachers and recorded in writing, because without it the saved time vanishes. Staff surveys give leaders a view of morale, workload and concerns, and AI features can help group open responses into themes, with a staff member checking the grouping. The results are shared with staff together with the actions leaders will take, since surveys that lead nowhere discourage honest answers. Retention analysis can help leaders see which staff may be at risk of leaving, and any such analysis must be used only to offer support such as mentoring, a schedule change or a conversation. The text does not give grade band variations for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels the evidence as mixed. A primary school study found planning time cut by more than half, but the saved time was absorbed by other demands (Carson et al., 2026). A review of automatic feedback found that nearly half of studies showed no reduction in instructor workload (Cavalcanti et al., 2021). These two findings are the evidence base the book offers for this idea, and they point in different directions rather than settling the question.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits here are set out plainly. Time savings are not real unless leaders decide, with teachers and in writing, where the saved time goes, because otherwise it disappears into other demands. Survey results should be shared with staff along with the actions leaders will take, and surveys that lead nowhere discourage honest answers. Retention analysis carries the strongest restriction: it must be used only to offer support, such as mentoring, a schedule change or a conversation, and it must never be used to make decisions about contracts or assignments. Staff should know how this data is used, so the decisions about support and about the use of staff data stay with people rather than being left to the analysis itself.
